title: BRICKSTORM Backdoor Investigation
description: Your organization has detected suspicious network activity originating from an internal host. Initial analysis suggests the presence of a backdoor malware named BRICKSTORM. Your task is to investigate the compromised host, identify the malicious activity, and contain the threat.
outcomes: Identify and investigate suspicious services and processes.
Analyze network connections for command-and-control communications.
Contain the threat by blocking malicious communications and removing persistence mechanisms.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: Your organization has detected suspicious network activity originating from an internal host. Initial analysis suggests the presence of a backdoor malware named BRICKSTORM. Your task is to investigate the compromised host, identify the malicious activity, and contain the threat.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: Access the sandbox environment via the provided cloud interface. Use the following credentials to log in: Username: cyrano, Password: cyrano. Enter the word 'start' to progress to the next level.
levels.local_content: Instructions for local sandbox usage. Enter the word 'start' to progress to the next level.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: While monitoring the network, you noticed unusual outbound connections from the host `target`. Investigate the running services on this host to identify any unauthorized or suspicious services. The flag you are looking for is the name of the suspicious service (string).
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious service, you can use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to list all running services. Look for any services that appear unusual or unauthorized. The suspicious service in this case is `updatemgr.service`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Suspicious services often have unusual names or descriptions. Look for services that do not match typical system services.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to list all running services and inspect them for any anomalies.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The suspicious service name starts with 'updatemgr'. Look for any services matching this pattern.

levels.title: C2 Communication Discovery (IP)
levels.content: The suspicious service identified in the previous task is likely communicating with a command-and-control (C2) server. Command-and-control servers are used by malware to receive instructions and exfiltrate data. Determine the remote IP address that the service is contacting. The flag you are looking for is the IP address of the C2 server (IPv4 address).
levels.solution: To determine the remote IP address, you can use network monitoring tools such as `netstat` or `ss` to inspect active connections. For example, the command `ss -tulnp` will show all active network connections. The IP address of the command-and-control server is `192.168.40.5`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Command-and-control communications typically involve outbound connections to external IP addresses. Look for connections to unusual or unknown IP addresses.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use network monitoring tools like `ss -tulnp` to inspect active connections and identify the destination IP address.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The C2 server IP address is in the range 192.168.40.0/24. Look for connections to this range.

levels.title: Process Termination
levels.content: To prevent further malicious activity, you need to stop the suspicious process associated with the backdoor. Malicious processes often have unusual names or descriptions. Identify and terminate the process while minimizing impact on legitimate services. The flag you are looking for is the name of the process that you terminated to stop the malicious activity (string).
levels.solution: To terminate the suspicious process, you can use the `pkill` command. For example, the command `pkill -f lab-checkin.sh` will terminate the process. The name of the process that you terminated to stop the malicious activity is `lab-checkin.sh`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Malicious processes often have unusual names or descriptions. Look for processes that do not match typical system processes.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use process management tools like `ps aux` or `pstree` to identify the malicious process and then use `pkill` to terminate it.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The malicious process name is `lab-checkin.sh`. Use `pkill -f lab-checkin.sh` to terminate it.
